lesson.title: Voltage: The Push Behind the Current
lesson.summary: This section explains voltage as the energy-per-charge difference between two points, showing why that difference is what makes charge move through a circuit whenever a path is available.
lesson.body:
You already know that electric charge is the fundamental property that lets particles attract or repel each other through the electric field surrounding them. Voltage is what tells you how much energy is tied up in moving a charge from one location to another inside that field. Formally, voltage is the difference in electric potential energy per unit of charge between two points, measured in volts, where one volt equals one joule of energy transferred for every coulomb of charge that moves between those points.

Think of it like elevation in a gravitational field. Two points on a hill differ in height, and that height difference determines how much energy a rock gains or loses falling between them - but height alone doesn't make the rock move; you need a path for it to roll down. Voltage works the same way for charge: two points in a circuit differ in electric potential, and that difference determines how much energy each coulomb of charge would gain or lose moving between them. But voltage by itself doesn't force charge to move - only when a conductive path connects those two points does the charge actually flow, releasing or absorbing energy as it travels.

This is also why voltage is always a comparison between two points, not a property of a single point on its own. Just as "height" alone means nothing without a reference (height above what?), a voltage value is meaningless unless you specify which two points you're comparing. When someone says a battery "is 9 volts," they really mean there's a 9-volt potential difference between its two terminals.

Let's make this concrete. Suppose you connect a 9-volt battery into a circuit, and over some interval, 2 coulombs of charge flow through the circuit from one terminal to the other. Since each coulomb gains 9 joules of energy crossing that potential difference, the total energy delivered to the circuit is 2 coulombs times 9 joules per coulomb, or 18 joules. That energy doesn't appear from nowhere - it comes from chemical reactions inside the battery that continually separate charge, piling up one type of charge at one terminal and depleting it at the other, and that ongoing separation is what maintains the 9-volt difference even as charge is drawn off and returned through the external circuit.

This picture also explains why voltage drives current whenever a path exists: the potential difference sets up an electric field along any conductor connecting the two points, and that field exerts a force on the mobile charges inside the conductor, pushing them along. A larger voltage between two points means a stronger push on each unit of charge, which is part of why bigger potential differences tend to drive more current through a given conductor - a relationship you'll pin down precisely once resistance enters the picture. For now, hold onto this core idea: charge is the "stuff" that moves, and voltage is the energy-per-charge difference that gives it a reason to move, the moment you give it somewhere to go.
